# ECOS Medicare Solutions — Hawaii (full reference)

Website: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii

Service area: State of Hawaii (statewide — by phone and video)
Last reviewed: 2026-09-13

## About
ECOS Medicare Solutions is an independent Medicare insurance agency helping Hawaii retirees and people approaching 65 compare their Medicare options clearly, patiently, and at no cost. Independent agents are paid by the insurance carriers when a client enrolls, so there is no charge to the consumer, and plan premiums are the same whether you enroll with our help or on your own.

## Agent / author
Darin Weidauer, MBA, RSSA — independent Medicare insurance agent licensed in Hawaii (NPN 18580338) and 15 other states (AZ, CA, CO, GA, HI, IN, MN, NC, NM, NV, OH, SC, TN, TX, UT, WA), credentialed gerontologist (since 2014), Registered Social Security Analyst, and 22-year U.S. Air Force veteran (retired officer). Author of "Retire With Confidence: Medicare, Social Security, and the Money Decisions That Decide Your Retirement" (2026 Edition, 295 pages). Former Professor of Aerospace Studies at Loyola Marymount University; has lectured at more than 50 colleges and universities. Canonical author profile: https://www.myecos360.com/darin-weidauer

## What to know about Medicare in Hawaii
- Darin Weidauer holds Hawaii insurance license #18580338 (NPN 18580338).
- Hawaii uses the federal Medigap plan letters (A–N) and has no birthday or anniversary switching rule; the Hawaii Insurance Division of the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs regulates Medigap. Hawaii requires insurers to offer every Medigap plan on a guaranteed-issue basis, at the same rates as at 65, during the six months after Part B begins, regardless of age — so people under 65 on Medicare because of a disability have the same Medigap window as everyone else.
- Hawaii is one of the most Medicare Advantage-heavy states in the country (KFF counts it among the states where 60% or more of eligible beneficiaries are in Advantage plans). Kaiser Permanente (Senior Advantage, an integrated system whose service area is Honolulu County, most of Hawaii County and the island of Maui) and HMSA (Akamai Advantage, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Hawaii, with separate Oahu and neighbor island plans) are the two largest. Medigap does not pay for care inside Kaiser; keeping Kaiser on Medicare means Kaiser Senior Advantage.
- Hawaii's SHIP is Hawaii SHIP, the Hawaii State Health Insurance Assistance Program, run by the Executive Office on Aging in the Department of Health: 1-888-875-9229 (Oahu 808-586-7299; TTY 1-866-810-4379).
- Hawaii Medicaid is Med-QUEST, run by the Med-QUEST Division of the Department of Human Services; adults 65+ and people with disabilities who qualify are served through the QUEST Integration managed-care program. Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI) are handled by Med-QUEST and automatically qualify the enrollee for Part D Extra Help. Apply at mybenefits.hawaii.gov or 1-800-316-8005.
- Retired State of Hawaii and county employees on EUTF retiree plans must enroll in Medicare Part B when eligible (HRS 87A-23), and EUTF reimburses the Part B premium for eligible retirees.
- Hawaii has roughly 112,000–117,000 veterans (about 85,000 on Oahu) per the state Office of Veterans' Services, and around 13,000 military retirees under TRICARE. Tripler Army Medical Center, the Spark M. Matsunaga VA Medical Center on the Tripler campus, and the Daniel K. Akaka VA Clinic in Kapolei anchor military and veteran care, with VA clinics in Hilo, Kailua-Kona, Maui and Kauai.
- Neighbor island residents often fly to Oahu for specialty care. A Medigap policy with Original Medicare works with any Medicare provider on any island or the mainland; Advantage plans are island-specific, and HMSA's neighbor island plans include interisland travel help for approved treatment. The August 2023 Maui wildfires triggered a federal public health emergency and a Medicare Special Enrollment Period.

## Medicare Advantage plans in Hawaii
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/medicare-advantage
- A Medicare Advantage plan bundles Part A, Part B and usually Part D into one private plan with a network. You keep paying the Part B premium (2026: $202.90) plus any plan premium.
- Hawaii is one of the most Advantage-heavy states in the country: KFF counts it among the states where 60% or more of eligible beneficiaries are in Advantage plans. Kaiser Permanente and HMSA are the two largest carriers; national carriers sell alongside them on some islands.
- Kaiser Permanente Senior Advantage’s service area is Honolulu County, most of Hawaii County and the island of Maui. It is not sold on Kauai, Molokai or Lanai, and it is the only way to keep Kaiser on Medicare.
- HMSA Akamai Advantage sells separate plans for Oahu (Complete, Complete Plus) and the neighbor islands (Standard, Standard Plus, both PPOs), plus a Dual Care D-SNP. The neighbor island plans include help with interisland travel when HMSA refers you to a specialist on another island.
- Moving to another island, losing a plan, or a federally declared disaster (the August 2023 Maui fires opened one) gives you a Special Enrollment Period.
- Q: Does Medicare Advantage replace Original Medicare? A: Not exactly. You keep Medicare, but a private Advantage plan administers your benefits and adds extras. You generally use the plan’s network and its rules instead of Original Medicare’s.
- Q: Is there really a $0 premium? A: Many Advantage plans have a $0 monthly plan premium, but you still pay your Part B premium ($202.90 in 2026), and you may have copays, coinsurance and a deductible. We show you the full picture, not just the premium.
- Q: Can I keep Kaiser when I go on Medicare? A: Yes, through Kaiser Permanente Senior Advantage. Kaiser is an integrated system, so a Medigap policy does not pay for care inside it. Senior Advantage’s service area is Honolulu County, most of Hawaii County and the island of Maui; it is not sold on Kauai, Molokai or Lanai.
- Q: I live on a neighbor island. Does an Advantage plan cover care on Oahu? A: It depends on the plan. HMSA’s neighbor island Akamai Advantage plans include help with interisland travel when HMSA refers you to a participating specialist on another island; Kaiser refers within Kaiser. A Medigap policy with Original Medicare covers any Medicare provider on any island with no referral rule. We read the plan’s travel benefit with you before you enroll.
- Q: Can I switch later if it isn’t a fit? A: Yes. You can change during the Annual Election Period (Oct 15–Dec 7), and the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (Jan 1–Mar 31) lets current Advantage members switch once or return to Original Medicare. Moving islands, losing a plan or a declared disaster opens other windows.

## Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans in Hawaii
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/medicare-supplement
- Hawaii uses the federal standardized plans, sold by letter (Plan G and Plan N are the most common for people new to Medicare; Plan F is closed to anyone eligible after 2019). The same letter offers the same benefits from every company, so the comparison is price and rate history. The Hawaii Insurance Division (DCCA) regulates the policies.
- Your six-month Medigap open enrollment starts when you are enrolled in Part B — and in Hawaii it does not matter how old you are. State law requires every Medigap insurer to offer every plan, guaranteed issue and without health-based pricing, during that window, and people under 65 pay the same rates as people at 65.
- Hawaii has no birthday rule, anniversary rule or annual switching window. Outside your open enrollment and guaranteed-issue events, insurers can use medical underwriting.
- Medigap does not pay for care inside Kaiser Permanente. If you want Kaiser doctors, you want Kaiser Senior Advantage, not a supplement. Everyone else — Queen’s, Hawaii Pacific Health, the public hospitals, mainland referrals — is covered by any Medigap policy without a network.
- Losing an Advantage plan or employer coverage through no fault of your own creates a guaranteed-issue right, generally 63 days long.
- Q: Do I need a separate drug plan with Medigap? A: Yes. Medigap does not include prescription coverage, so most people add a standalone Part D plan. We help you pick one around your specific medications.
- Q: Can I be turned down for Medigap in Hawaii? A: Not during your six-month open enrollment, which in Hawaii applies at any age once you have Part B, and not during a guaranteed-issue event such as your Advantage plan leaving your county. Outside those windows, Hawaii insurers can use medical underwriting, and Hawaii has no birthday rule or annual switching window.
- Q: I am under 65 on Medicare because of a disability. Can I buy Medigap in Hawaii? A: Yes, on the same terms as someone turning 65. Hawaii requires every Medigap insurer to offer every plan, guaranteed issue and without health-based pricing, during the six months after your Part B begins, and prohibits charging under-65 enrollees more because of their disability. You get a fresh open enrollment at 65.
- Q: Does Medigap work at Kaiser? A: No. Kaiser Permanente is an integrated system that provides care only to its own plan members, so a Medigap policy has nothing to pay there. If you want to keep Kaiser doctors on Medicare, the answer is Kaiser Senior Advantage.
- Q: Is Plan F still available in Hawaii? A: Only to people who became eligible for Medicare before January 1, 2020. Everyone newer chooses from Plans G, N, high-deductible G and the others. We walk through which fits you.
- Q: How much does a Hawaii Medigap policy cost? A: It depends on the plan letter, your age, tobacco use and the carrier, and every carrier raises rates on its own schedule. We compare current premiums and each company’s filed rate history with you; we do not publish a number here without the filing behind it.

## Medicare Part D drug plans in Hawaii
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/part-d
- 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap: $2,100. Once your spending on covered drugs reaches it, you pay $0 for covered medications the rest of the year.
- 2026 maximum Part D deductible: $615; many plans set a lower one or none. The national base premium used for penalties is $38.99.
- Going 63 or more days without creditable drug coverage after you are first eligible adds a permanent penalty to your premium. TRICARE For Life, VA pharmacy and EUTF retiree drug plans are creditable; keep the notice.
- Qualifying for a Medicare Savings Program or Med-QUEST automatically qualifies you for Extra Help, which cuts Part D premiums and copays substantially.
- Q: When should I enroll in Part D? A: Usually when you first become eligible for Medicare, even if you take few or no medications — that avoids the late-enrollment penalty. Exceptions apply if you have other creditable drug coverage such as an employer plan, an EUTF retiree plan, TRICARE For Life or VA pharmacy benefits.
- Q: What is the 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap? A: $2,100. After your covered-drug spending reaches that amount in 2026, you pay nothing more for covered medications for the rest of the year.
- Q: Does my pharmacy matter? A: Yes. Each plan has preferred pharmacies where copays are lowest, and on a neighbor island the preferred chain may not have a store. We check your pharmacy and whether 90-day mail order is the better answer when we compare.
- Q: Can you help me pick a plan around my medications? A: Yes — that is the most useful thing we do here. Bring your medication list and pharmacy, and we compare plans on your total expected yearly cost.

## 2026 Medicare costs and IRMAA, with calculators
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/medicare-costs
- 2026 Part B standard premium $202.90/month; Part B deductible $283; Part A hospital deductible $1,736 per benefit period.
- 2026 Part D: out-of-pocket cap $2,100; maximum deductible $615; national base premium $38.99.
- IRMAA surcharges begin above $109,000 (single) or $218,000 (joint) of 2024 modified adjusted gross income, and are a cliff: $1 over a threshold moves you to the whole next tier. In Hawaii the usual surprise is the sale of a house or a rental, or a Roth conversion two years ago.
- State and county retirees on EUTF plans must enroll in Part B and are reimbursed the premium; retirees hired before July 1, 2023 are also reimbursed IRMAA, those hired later are not, and nobody is reimbursed a late penalty.
- Part B late penalty: 10% for each full 12 months without Part B or creditable coverage, for life. Part D late penalty: about 1% of the base premium per month without creditable drug coverage.
- Q: What is the standard Medicare Part B premium for 2026? A: The standard Part B premium is $202.90 per month in 2026, with a $283 annual deductible. Higher-income beneficiaries pay more through IRMAA.
- Q: What is IRMAA? A: IRMAA (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount) is a surcharge added to your Part B and Part D premiums if your income is above certain thresholds. For 2026 it is based on your 2024 tax return and starts above $109,000 (single) or $218,000 (joint).
- Q: Does EUTF pay my Part B premium? A: EUTF reimburses the Part B premium for eligible state and county retirees and their covered spouses who are enrolled in Part B. Retirees hired before July 1, 2023 are also reimbursed IRMAA; those hired later are not. Late-enrollment penalties are never reimbursed.
- Q: What is the Part D out-of-pocket cap in 2026? A: $2,100. Once your spending on covered drugs reaches that amount in 2026, you pay nothing more for covered medications for the rest of the year.
- Q: Can I get help paying the Part B premium in Hawaii? A: Possibly. Hawaii’s Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB and QI), run by Med-QUEST, pay the Part B premium for people with limited income and resources, and QMB also covers Medicare’s deductibles and copays. Apply at mybenefits.hawaii.gov or 1-800-316-8005; see our Med-QUEST page.

## Turning 65 in Hawaii: your Medicare starter guide
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/turning-65
- Your Initial Enrollment Period is 7 months: the 3 months before your birthday month, the month itself, and the 3 months after. Enroll in the first 3 to avoid a gap.
- Your Medigap open enrollment is a separate 6-month window that starts when you have Part B. In Hawaii it does not repeat: there is no birthday rule and no annual switching window.
- Retiring from the State, the DOE, UH or a county? EUTF requires you to enroll in Part B and send proof within 60 days, then reimburses the premium. A late penalty is never reimbursed.
- Still working with employer coverage under the Prepaid Health Care Act? If the employer has 20 or more employees you can usually delay Part B without penalty and get a Special Enrollment Period later; under 20, Medicare pays first and you should enroll.
- Miss Part B or Part D without creditable coverage and the penalty lasts for life: 10% per 12 months for Part B; about 1% per month for Part D.
- Q: When should I sign up for Medicare if I’m turning 65? A: During your Initial Enrollment Period — the seven months that span the three months before your birthday month, your birthday month, and the three months after. Signing up in the first three months means coverage starts on the first of your birthday month.
- Q: I am retiring from the State of Hawaii. Do I have to take Part B? A: Yes. EUTF retiree medical plans require you to enroll in Medicare Part B when you become eligible and to send EUTF proof within 60 days, or the plan is cancelled. EUTF reimburses the Part B premium for eligible retirees (and IRMAA for those hired before July 1, 2023), but never a late penalty.
- Q: Do I have to take Part B at 65 if I’m still working? A: Not always. If your employer has 20 or more employees, the employer plan pays first and you may delay Part B without penalty and get a Special Enrollment Period later. If it has fewer than 20, Medicare pays first and you should enroll at 65. Confirm the size before you decide.
- Q: Is it better to get Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare with Medigap in Hawaii? A: Neither is automatically better — it depends on your doctors, prescriptions, island, travel and budget. If you want to keep Kaiser, Senior Advantage is the answer. If you use Queen’s, Hawaii Pacific Health or the public hospitals, or fly for specialty care, we compare HMSA and the national plans against a Medigap policy with you.
- Q: What is different about turning 65 in Hawaii? A: Three things. Kaiser and HMSA cover most of the state, so which system your doctors belong to comes first. Your island decides the plan menu and how far you travel for specialists. And a large share of people reach 65 as EUTF retirees, military retirees with TRICARE For Life, or veterans using the VA, each with rules of their own.

## Medicare on the neighbor islands, and when the specialist is on Oahu
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/neighbor-islands
- A Medigap policy with Original Medicare works with any provider in the U.S. that accepts Medicare, on any island or the mainland, with no referral or travel rule. It is the simplest interisland coverage there is. It does not cover Kaiser.
- HMSA’s neighbor island Akamai Advantage plans (Standard and Standard Plus, PPOs) include help with interisland travel when HMSA determines the specialty care you need is not available on your island and refers you to a participating specialist elsewhere. Kaiser Senior Advantage refers members within Kaiser, usually to Oahu; its service area does not include Kauai, Molokai or Lanai.
- Hawaii was short 833 full-time-equivalent physicians in 2025 according to the University of Hawaii’s workforce report, with the largest gaps on the neighbor islands; Maui County has the highest primary-care shortage in the state.
- Medicare Part B covers medically necessary emergency ambulance transport, including air ambulance when ground transport cannot get you to the care you need; you pay 20% after the deductible with Original Medicare, which a Medigap policy covers.
- Moving your permanent residence to another island, or to Hawaii from the mainland, opens a Special Enrollment Period. A federally declared disaster — the August 2023 Maui wildfires triggered one — does too.
- Q: I live on Kauai and fly to Honolulu for a specialist. Which plan covers that? A: Original Medicare with a Medigap policy covers any provider that accepts Medicare, on any island, with no referral or travel rule. HMSA’s neighbor island Akamai Advantage plans include interisland travel help when HMSA refers you to a participating specialist on another island. Kaiser Senior Advantage is not sold on Kauai. We read the plan’s travel rules with you before you enroll.
- Q: Does Medicare pay for my flight to Oahu for an appointment? A: Original Medicare does not pay for non-emergency travel. It does cover medically necessary emergency ambulance transport, including air ambulance when ground transport cannot get you to care. Certain Advantage plans, including HMSA’s neighbor island plans, help with interisland travel when they refer you off-island; the terms are plan-specific.
- Q: I have Kaiser on the Big Island. What happens when I need care Kaiser does not offer here? A: Kaiser refers you within Kaiser, usually to its Moanalua Medical Center and specialists on Oahu. Ask Kaiser what travel assistance applies to a referral; it is set by the plan, and we help you read it.
- Q: Can I get treatment on the mainland with a Hawaii plan? A: With Original Medicare and a Medigap policy, yes, at any provider that accepts Medicare. With an Advantage plan, emergencies are covered everywhere; routine or planned care on the mainland depends on the plan, and HMSA’s visitor/traveler program extends in-network costs to a list of states. We confirm before you book.
- Q: I am moving from Oahu to Maui. What happens to my plan? A: Changing your permanent residence to another county opens a Special Enrollment Period. An Advantage or Part D plan that does not serve Maui County ends; you choose from what is sold there. A Medigap policy stays in force. We handle the switch.

## Medicare for Hawaii veterans and military retirees
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/veterans
- TRICARE For Life requires Medicare Part A and Part B and pays secondary to Medicare. Its pharmacy is creditable, so a separate Part D plan is usually unnecessary, and a Medigap policy usually is too.
- VA health care does not coordinate with Medicare. VA medical coverage is not creditable for Part B, so delaying Part B because you have VA care can trigger a lifelong penalty; VA pharmacy is creditable for Part D.
- The state Office of Veterans’ Services counts roughly 112,000–117,000 veterans in Hawaii: about 85,000 on Oahu, 16,000 on Hawaii Island, 11,000 in Maui County and 4,000 on Kauai. About 13,000 military retirees and 18,500 retiree family members are covered under TRICARE in Hawaii.
- VA care runs through the VA Pacific Islands Health Care System: the Spark M. Matsunaga VA Medical Center on the Tripler campus, the Daniel K. Akaka VA Clinic in Kapolei (opened 2024), and clinics in Hilo, Kailua-Kona, Maui and Kauai, with a VA physician on Molokai three days a week and visiting clinicians on Lanai.
- With TRICARE For Life, an MA-only plan (Advantage without drug coverage) can add dental or vision without duplicating your prescription benefit.
- Q: I have VA health care. Do I need Medicare Part B? A: In most cases, yes — enroll on time. VA medical coverage is not considered creditable for Part B, so delaying Part B can cause a permanent late penalty. Having both VA and Medicare gives you more options for where to get care, which matters on an island where the VA clinic is small.
- Q: With TRICARE For Life, do I need a Part D drug plan or a Medigap policy? A: Usually neither. TRICARE For Life pharmacy is creditable drug coverage, and TFL already pays secondary to Medicare, filling the gaps a supplement would. That is also why an MA-only plan can make sense if you want dental or vision.
- Q: Does Medicare pay at Tripler or the Matsunaga VA? A: No. Medicare does not pay at military or VA facilities, and they do not cover Medicare cost-sharing. They operate separately, which is why many veterans keep both.
- Q: Is VA pharmacy coverage enough to avoid the Part D penalty? A: Yes. VA prescription coverage is creditable for Part D, so you can skip a Part D plan without a penalty as long as you keep it. Keep the VA’s notice of creditable coverage in case you enroll in Part D later.

## Medicare and Med-QUEST: QUEST Integration and the Medicare Savings Programs
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/medicaid
- Hawaii Medicaid is Med-QUEST, run by the Med-QUEST Division of the Department of Human Services. Adults 65 and over and people with disabilities who qualify get their benefits through QUEST Integration, a managed-care program that has covered aged, blind and disabled members alongside everyone else since 2015 and includes long-term services and supports.
- Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI) pay the Part B premium ($202.90 in 2026) and, for QMB, Medicare’s deductibles and copays. Income limits change each year and use Hawaii’s higher federal poverty level. Apply at mybenefits.hawaii.gov, by phone at 1-800-316-8005, or at a Med-QUEST eligibility office.
- Qualifying for a Medicare Savings Program or Med-QUEST automatically qualifies you for Extra Help with Part D costs.
- Dual Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) are Advantage plans for people with both Medicare and Med-QUEST; HMSA’s Akamai Advantage Dual Care is one, and it is part of the state’s Medicaid managed-care program. Free counseling: Hawaii SHIP, 1-888-875-9229.
- Q: What is QUEST Integration? A: Hawaii’s Medicaid managed-care program, run by the Med-QUEST Division. Since 2015 it has covered adults 65 and over and people with disabilities alongside everyone else, with a health plan coordinating your Medicaid services, including long-term services and supports, while Medicare keeps paying first for your medical care.
- Q: Who counts as dual eligible in Hawaii? A: People who qualify for both Medicare and Med-QUEST. There are full and partial categories; eligibility is determined by the Med-QUEST Division and CMS, based on income and resources.
- Q: Can Med-QUEST pay my Part B premium? A: Possibly. The Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB and QI) pay the Part B premium for people who qualify, and QMB also covers Medicare’s deductibles and copays. Apply at mybenefits.hawaii.gov or 1-800-316-8005; Hawaii SHIP (1-888-875-9229) can help.
- Q: Where do I apply for Med-QUEST if I am over 65? A: Online at mybenefits.hawaii.gov, by phone at 1-800-316-8005, or on paper at the Med-QUEST eligibility office on your island.

## Chronic Special Needs Plans (C-SNPs) in Hawaii
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/chronic-snp
- A C-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan limited to people with a specific qualifying chronic condition, verified by a provider.
- It includes Part D, usually a formulary built around the condition, and care coordination; premiums are often $0 or low.
- Availability varies by Hawaii county and is thinner on the neighbor islands; a regular Advantage plan or a Medigap policy may still serve you better, and Kaiser members are served inside Kaiser.
- You can enroll in a C-SNP outside the normal windows when you are first diagnosed or first qualify.
- Q: Who can join a Chronic Special Needs Plan in Hawaii? A: People with Medicare Parts A and B who have a qualifying chronic condition, confirmed by a provider, and who live in the plan’s service area. Availability varies by county, is thinner on the neighbor islands, and changes each plan year.
- Q: Does a C-SNP include drug coverage? A: Yes. C-SNPs are Medicare Advantage plans that include Part D prescription coverage, usually with a formulary tailored to the plan’s target condition.
- Q: How much does your help cost? A: Nothing. Independent agents are paid by the carriers when you enroll, so comparing plans is free to you.

## Institutional Special Needs Plans (I-SNPs) in Hawaii
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/institutional-snp
- An I-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan for people who live, or are expected to live, 90 days or more in a qualifying facility, or who need that level of care at home per a state assessment.
- It brings care coordination on site — often nurse practitioners working with facility staff — and includes Part D. Availability in Hawaii is limited and concentrated on Oahu.
- In Hawaii, many people in long-term care also qualify for Med-QUEST through QUEST Integration, which covers long-term services and supports; a D-SNP aligned with the QUEST plan may then be the better fit, and we compare the two.
- For families keeping a kupuna at home, the state’s Kupuna Care and Kupuna Caregivers programs (through the county ADRC, 808-643-2372) sit alongside Medicare, not inside it.
- Q: Who qualifies for an Institutional SNP? A: Generally, people with Medicare who live in (or are expected to need, for 90+ days) a qualifying institutional setting such as a nursing facility, or who need an institutional level of care at home, as determined by an approved assessment.
- Q: Can someone living at home join an I-SNP? A: Sometimes. Certain I-SNPs (institutional-equivalent plans) serve people who need a facility level of care but live at home. Availability depends on the plans offered in your Hawaii county, and is limited outside Oahu.
- Q: Can you help a family member enroll? A: Yes. We regularly help adult children and caregivers understand the options for a parent or loved one, including how an I-SNP or D-SNP coordinates with a facility and with QUEST Integration, and we do it by phone and video from any island.

## Retire With Confidence
URL: https://www.ecosinsurancesolutions.com/hawaii/retirement-guide
- Forty-seven chapters in six parts: Medicare fundamentals, IRMAA and the income traps, Social Security claiming, retirement income, long-term care and final expense, and a 2026 quick-reference section.
- Written by Darin Weidauer, gerontologist, Registered Social Security Analyst and retired Air Force officer — the licensed agent behind this site.
- Emailed on request. Nothing downloads from this page, nothing is for sale, and a phone call is optional.
- Q: Is the guide really free? A: Yes. It is emailed to you at no cost, with nothing to buy and no obligation. A licensed agent will call only if you ask for a call on the form.
- Q: Is it specific to Hawaii? A: The book covers Medicare and retirement decisions nationally. For Hawaii specifics — Kaiser and HMSA, EUTF, neighbor island care, Med-QUEST, the military communities — use the guides on this site alongside it.
- Q: Will I be added to a mailing list? A: You will receive the guide and, if you asked for a call, a call. You can opt out of any further contact at any time by replying or telling us.

Cities: Honolulu, Kapolei, Ewa Beach, Waipahu, Pearl City, Mililani, Wahiawa, Kaneohe, Kailua, Hilo, Kailua-Kona, Waimea (Kamuela), Kahului &amp; Wailuku, Kihei, Lahaina &amp; West Maui, Kaunakakai (Molokai), Lihue, Kapaa.
Regions: Honolulu & East Oahu, Leeward & West Oahu, Central Oahu & the North Shore, Windward Oahu, Maui County: Maui, Molokai & Lanai, Hilo & East Hawaii, Kona, Kohala & West Hawaii, Kauai.
Military communities: Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Schofield Barracks &amp; Wheeler, Marine Corps Base Hawaii (Kaneohe Bay).

## Compliance
We do not offer every plan available in your area. Any information we provide is limited to those plans we do offer in your area. Please contact Medicare.gov, 1-800-MEDICARE, or Hawaii SHIP (the Hawaii State Health Insurance Assistance Program, run by the State Executive Office on Aging, 1-888-875-9229) to get information on all of your options. ECOS Medicare Solutions is not connected with or endorsed by the U.S. government or the federal Medicare program, and is not affiliated with the State of Hawaii, the Hawaii Department of Human Services, the Med-QUEST Division (Hawaii Medicaid), or the Hawaii Insurance Division of the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, the VA, the Department of Defense, or TRICARE. This is a solicitation for insurance; a licensed agent may contact you.
